source.title: Efficient Language Modeling for Low-Resource Settings with Hybrid RNN-Transformer Architectures
source.authors: Gabriel Lindenmaier; Sean Papay; Sebastian Padó

record.tranche_reason: The study compares language-model losses across architectures at roughly comparable parameter counts, bearing on whether architecture details have little effect. It does not reproduce the original scaling-law sweeps.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own held-out language-modeling results for three architectures on Enwik8, WikiText-103 and PG-19. These architecture comparisons bear on V4; they do not test power-law scaling, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation. Comparisons to prior-work models are cited results and are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures held-out language-modeling loss across three architectures at approximately matched parameter counts, directly bearing on V4. It does not fit or extrapolate scaling laws.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately captures the main conclusion: adding initial QRNN blocks can improve parameter efficiency and language-modeling performance, especially for the Hybrid Transformer. The authors leave higher-resource scaling unresolved. Their approximately 100M-token limitation describes the main Enwik8/WikiText experiments; Appendix B additionally evaluates the larger PG-19 corpus.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares recurrent-attention hybrid architectures with a PAR Transformer baseline; it does not apply the original scaling-law fitting or compute-optimal allocation method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported PG-19 ordering and performance gaps are examined across tokenizations and vocabulary sizes; the authors state that the gap between models increases for decreasing token lengths. WikiText-103 PPL comparisons are described as not significantly different, unlike the reported Enwik8 and PG-19 comparisons.
record.problems: Only a low-resource setting is studied, with roughly 100M-token corpora and models around 40M parameters (excluding embeddings); the authors state that scaling to higher-resource regimes remains unexamined. Results are single fixed-seed runs. The architecture comparisons do not independently sweep depth, width, or other architectural dimensions.
record.rows_left_out: No own result rows were omitted. Comparisons to models from cited prior work were excluded because they are not results generated by this study.

untested.parts: No multiscale parameter, token, or compute sweep establishes a power-law loss curve.
No small-run fit predicts larger-run loss.
No compute-budget allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token exponents.

No independent depth or width sweep, broad parameter range, or higher-resource architecture comparison. Parameter counts are approximately matched, and architecture-specific hyperparameters also differ.
No power-law fits in other modalities or training regimes; repeated training alone does not test this version.
No downstream tasks or relationship between downstream performance and scale or pretraining loss.
No fitted scaling exponents, compute-optimal splits, or curve-bending analysis across setup or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: V4 permits slight loss differences, so statistical significance alone is insufficient for a limits_scope verdict. Here supports means compatibility with modest loss sensitivity in the tested comparisons, not proof of architecture invariance across a wide range. Training uses single fixed-seed runs, approximately matched parameter counts and fixed training time, with architecture-specific hyperparameters and unequal update counts. Alternative bits-per-byte and perplexity columns largely restate the recorded predictive-loss measurements.

versions.untested_parts: No scaling sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute, and no fit of a power law.
No small-run fit or prediction of larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or fitted parameter/token trends.
Only a few specific architectures are compared; depth, width, and architecture are not independently varied over a wide range.
All experiments are text language modeling; no other modality or training regime is tested.
No downstream task performance is measured.
No scaling exponents or compute-optimal split are fitted or compared across fitting choices.
